[2018 summer phd math-stat — problem 1]

We observe a single discrete random variable $X$ with pmf $f_\theta(x) = P_\theta(X = x)$ given by $f_\theta(0) = \theta/6$, $f_\theta(1) = \theta/2$, $f_\theta(2) = 1 - \theta$, $f_\theta(3) = \theta/3$, with parameter space $\Theta = \{\theta : 0 \le \theta \le 1\}$.
(a) Does this family have the monotone likelihood ratio property in $x$? Prove or disprove.
(b) Test $H_0 : \theta \le 1/4$ vs $H_1 : \theta > 1/4$. (i) Does a UMP level-$\alpha$ test exist? Prove or disprove; if so find it and establish it is UMP level $\alpha$. (ii) Using Uniform$[0,1]$ as a prior for $\theta$, what is the size of the Bayes test procedure?
(c) Does a complete sufficient statistic exist? If so, find it and prove completeness and sufficiency.
(d) Does a UMVUE of $\theta$ exist? Prove or disprove; if so obtain it and establish it is a UMVUE.

response.text:
Let  
\[
A=\{0,1,3\},\qquad T=\mathbf 1_A(X)=\mathbf 1\{X\neq 2\}.
\]
Then
\[
P_\theta(T=1)=P_\theta(X\in A)=\theta,\qquad P_\theta(T=0)=1-\theta.
\]

## (a) Monotone likelihood ratio in \(x\)

For \(0<\theta_1<\theta_2<1\), the likelihood ratio is

\[
\frac{f_{\theta_2}(x)}{f_{\theta_1}(x)}
=
\begin{cases}
\theta_2/\theta_1, & x=0,1,3,\\[4pt]
(1-\theta_2)/(1-\theta_1), & x=2.
\end{cases}
\]

Since \(\theta_2>\theta_1\),

\[
\frac{\theta_2}{\theta_1}>1
\qquad\text{but}\qquad
\frac{1-\theta_2}{1-\theta_1}<1.
\]

Thus, for example,

\[
\frac{f_{\theta_2}(1)}{f_{\theta_1}(1)}
=
\frac{\theta_2}{\theta_1}
>
\frac{1-\theta_2}{1-\theta_1}
=
\frac{f_{\theta_2}(2)}{f_{\theta_1}(2)}.
\]

Because \(1<2\), this violates nondecreasingness in \(x\). Therefore the family does **not** have the monotone likelihood ratio property in \(x\).

---

## (b) Testing \(H_0:\theta\le 1/4\) versus \(H_1:\theta>1/4\)

Let \(\theta_0=1/4\). A randomized test is a function \(\phi:\{0,1,2,3\}\to[0,1]\), where \(\phi(x)\) is the probability of rejecting \(H_0\) after observing \(X=x\).

### (i) UMP level-\(\alpha\) test

A UMP level-\(\alpha\) test exists. It is based on \(T=\mathbf 1\{X\neq 2\}\).

For \(0\le \alpha\le 1/4\), define

\[
\phi_\alpha(x)=
\begin{cases}
4\alpha, & x\in\{0,1,3\},\\
0, & x=2.
\end{cases}
\]

For \(1/4<\alpha\le 1\), define

\[
\phi_\alpha(x)=
\begin{cases}
1, & x\in\{0,1,3\},\\[4pt]
\dfrac{4\alpha-1}{3}, & x=2.
\end{cases}
\]

Equivalently, in terms of \(T\),

\[
\phi_\alpha(T)=
\begin{cases}
4\alpha\, T, & 0\le \alpha\le 1/4,\\[6pt]
T+\dfrac{4\alpha-1}{3}(1-T), & 1/4<\alpha\le 1.
\end{cases}
\]

Check the size.

If \(0\le \alpha\le 1/4\), then

\[
E_\theta[\phi_\alpha(X)]
=
4\alpha P_\theta(X\in A)
=
4\alpha\theta.
\]

Thus

\[
\sup_{\theta\le 1/4} E_\theta[\phi_\alpha(X)]
=
4\alpha\cdot \frac14
=
\alpha.
\]

If \(1/4<\alpha\le 1\), then

\[
E_\theta[\phi_\alpha(X)]
=
P_\theta(X\in A)+\frac{4\alpha-1}{3}P_\theta(X=2)
=
\theta+\frac{4\alpha-1}{3}(1-\theta).
\]

This is increasing in \(\theta\), so its supremum over \(\theta\le 1/4\) occurs at \(\theta=1/4\). Hence

\[
\sup_{\theta\le 1/4} E_\theta[\phi_\alpha(X)]
=
\frac14+\frac{4\alpha-1}{3}\cdot \frac34
=
\alpha.
\]

So \(\phi_\alpha\) has level \(\alpha\).

To prove UMP, fix any \(\theta_1>1/4\). Consider the simple-vs-simple test of \(\theta=\theta_0=1/4\) against \(\theta=\theta_1\). The likelihood ratio is

\[
\frac{f_{\theta_1}(x)}{f_{\theta_0}(x)}
=
\begin{cases}
4\theta_1, & x\in\{0,1,3\},\\[4pt]
\dfrac{4(1-\theta_1)}{3}, & x=2.
\end{cases}
\]

Since \(\theta_1>1/4\),

\[
4\theta_1>\frac{4(1-\theta_1)}{3}.
\]

Thus the Neyman-Pearson most powerful level-\(\alpha\) test rejects first on \(A=\{0,1,3\}\), with randomization as above. Importantly, this rejection rule does not depend on the particular \(\theta_1>1/4\). Therefore the same test is most powerful against every simple alternative \(\theta_1>1/4\).

Since \(\phi_\alpha\) also has level \(\alpha\) for the composite null \(H_0:\theta\le 1/4\), it is UMP level \(\alpha\).

---

### (ii) Size of the Bayes test using a Uniform\([0,1]\) prior

Assume the usual Bayes rule under equal \(0\)-\(1\) loss: reject \(H_0\) if

\[
P(\theta>1/4\mid X=x)>P(\theta\le 1/4\mid X=x).
\]

With the prior \(\theta\sim \mathrm{Unif}[0,1]\), for \(x\in A=\{0,1,3\}\),

\[
\pi(\theta\mid x)\propto \theta,
\]

so the posterior density is \(2\theta\). Therefore

\[
P(\theta\le 1/4\mid x)
=
\int_0^{1/4}2\theta\,d\theta
=
\frac1{16},
\]

and hence \(P(\theta>1/4\mid x)=15/16\). Thus the Bayes test rejects \(H_0\) for \(x\in A\).

For \(x=2\),

\[
\pi(\theta\mid X=2)\propto 1-\theta,
\]

so the posterior density is \(2(1-\theta)\). Therefore

\[
P(\theta\le 1/4\mid X=2)
=
\int_0^{1/4}2(1-\theta)\,d\theta
=
\frac{7}{16},
\]

while

\[
P(\theta>1/4\mid X=2)=\frac9{16}.
\]

Thus the Bayes test also rejects \(H_0\) when \(X=2\). Therefore the Bayes test rejects for every possible observation.

Hence its frequentist size is

\[
\sup_{\theta\le 1/4} P_\theta(\text{reject }H_0)=1.
\]

So the Bayes test has size \(1\).

---

## (c) Complete sufficient statistic

The statistic

\[
T=\mathbf 1\{X\neq 2\}
\]

is sufficient. Indeed, define

\[
h(0)=\frac16,\qquad h(1)=\frac12,\qquad h(2)=1,\qquad h(3)=\frac13.
\]

Then

\[
f_\theta(x)=h(x)\theta^{T(x)}(1-\theta)^{1-T(x)}.
\]

By the Neyman-Fisher factorization theorem, \(T\) is sufficient.

Now \(T\sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(\theta)\). To prove completeness, suppose \(g\) is any function on \(\{0,1\}\) such that

\[
E_\theta[g(T)]=0
\]

for all \(0\le \theta\le 1\). Then

\[
E_\theta[g(T)]
=
(1-\theta)g(0)+\theta g(1)=0
\]

for all \(\theta\in[0,1]\). Taking \(\theta=0\) gives \(g(0)=0\), and taking \(\theta=1\) gives \(g(1)=0\). Therefore \(g(T)=0\) almost surely for all \(\theta\).

Thus \(T=\mathbf 1\{X\neq 2\}\) is complete and sufficient.

---

## (d) UMVUE of \(\theta\)

Since

\[
E_\theta[T]=P_\theta(X\neq 2)=\theta,
\]

the statistic

\[
\widehat\theta=T=\mathbf 1\{X\neq 2\}
\]

is unbiased for \(\theta\).

By part (c), \(T\) is complete and sufficient. Therefore, by the Lehmann-Scheffé theorem, any unbiased estimator that is a function of \(T\) is the unique UMVUE. Since \(T\) itself is unbiased for \(\theta\), it is the UMVUE.

Thus the UMVUE is

\[
\boxed{\widehat\theta=\mathbf 1\{X\neq 2\}}.
\]
